item.title: NASA’s Artemis II Moon Mission Research Continues on Earth - NASA Science (.gov)
item.description:
Since NASA’s Artemis II crew members safely splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on April 10 after their record-setting mission around the Moon, science teams have been busy collecting more data and combing through observations collected on the test flight. Results from these science investigations will help support safe human exploration of deep space and provide a blueprint for how future missions will conduct science on the lunar surface as NASA builds a Moon Base and develops an enduring human presence there.

Postflight crew health, performance data

In the hours, days, and weeks after landing, the Artemis II crew members, NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, contributed critical data to help the agency understand how the human body reacts to spaceflight. Collecting this data as soon as possible after landing was important to understand how the body adapts from microgravity to Earth’s gravity. The data will inform NASA’s understanding of how quickly crews can complete mission-critical tasks after landing on a planetary surface like the Moon or Mars, where there won’t be landing support personnel to assist.

Within a day of splashdown, researchers collected a suite of data for the Artemis II Spaceflight Standard Measures study, which is part of a larger effort across the astronaut corps to gather a baseline set of health measurements on blood pressure, heart rate, eye health, and motor control. Crew members also completed a mini obstacle course, which included lying down, standing up, unfurling a rope ladder, ladder climbing, and more, to assess how their bodies were adapting to Earth’s gravity.

Once the crew returned to NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, researchers guided them through further medical check-ups and tests of motor control. Over the next several days, the crew completed obstacle courses wearing spacesuits offloaded to lunar gravity, which is roughly one-sixth the force of Earth’s gravity. Researchers are now analyzing this data to gain insight into how crews may perform as they adapt to the gravity of a planetary surface.

As part of the Immune Biomarkers study, researchers are comparing blood and saliva samples collected after the Artemis II splashdown with samples collected preflight and during the mission. Among other topics, the study investigates whether and how dormant viruses reawaken in astronauts’ bodies while in space.

Some crew members completed postflight cognition tests and a simulated manual spacecraft docking task to assess motor control for the ARCHeR (Artemis Research for Crew Health & Readiness) study. This, combined with data collected through a wrist-worn device while crew members were in space, is used to understand the effect of space hazards on well-being and performance.

Initial data collections for Artemis II health studies concluded 45 days after splashdown. However, medical teams will continually monitor astronaut health throughout the Artemis II crew members’ lifetimes.

Once this data is processed and anonymized, information will be available for scientists to study the effects of spaceflight via a request to NASA’s Life Sciences Data Archive. The results from this work could lead to new technologies and studies that help predict the adaptability of crews on future missions to the Moon and Mars.

Analyzing astronaut-derived organ chips flown around Moon

Organ chips from NASA’s AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation are being analyzed at chip developer Emulate's laboratory in Boston. The organ chips included bone marrow cells from each Artemis II astronaut. They flew around the Moon with the astronauts, and now researchers are studying these organ chips to determine how deep space radiation and microgravity affect human health at the molecular level.

Scientists are comparing the chips flown aboard the spacecraft to ground controls and crew blood samples using advanced techniques, including single-cell RNA sequencing. The analysis will characterize how organ chips model individual responses to spaceflight, which is data that could allow NASA to send future astronauts’ AVATAR chips ahead on missions to develop personalized medical kits. The researchers plan to share early findings at scientific conferences while full analysis continues.

Lunar imagery, audio for data release

On April 6, the Artemis II crew members studied features on and around the Moon for nearly seven hours during Orion’s closest approach to the lunar surface. Their work was guided by a minute-by-minute observation plan developed by the Artemis II lunar science team.

Scientists are reviewing the data collected from the mission, which includes images, video, and audio files, to release a report of their initial data interpretations later this year. The report will cover observations of impact flashes, variations in color on the lunar surface, and the shape and texture of faults and ridges. The team also will publish a report on how Artemis II lunar science observations were planned, organized, and executed for the benefit of future Artemis missions.

NASA will publish more than 100 science-related audio recordings with transcripts, as well as approximately 11,500 Earth and Moon image and video files from the mission science campaign, with accompanying data. While many of these images already are public, these records will be available through NASA’s Planetary Data System, a public archive of data from all of NASA’s planetary missions. To get the data ready, the team is converting files into standard formats that anyone can easily open and add information to make the data searchable in NASA’s archive for generations to come.

item.title: The Artemis II Effect: When Everyone Is Brilliant, Character Becomes The Mission - forbes.com
item.description:
Something genuinely pure is happening on the internet this week. People are obsessed. Not over celebrity gossip or political outrage, but over four astronauts in a capsule the size of a minivan, 250,000 miles from Earth, being decent with each other and radiating that joy and camaraderie back to us in real time.

I’ve been watching this mission the way I know millions of others have: not as a space anything, because honestly I have zero interest in space, and yet here I am, because I needed a damn break. Earth is exhausting. And what started as escapism became something else entirely. Underneath the awe, I keep feeling pure joy. Not inspiration as a concept. Joy as a physical experience. Yes, I’m randomly crying at a response they make to a kid or a photo they release. That reaction, happening at scale, across every platform, is itself a form of power. And it is worth understanding why.

The Artemis II mission launched on April 1 and splashes down tomorrow. You already know the exciting headlines: first crewed lunar mission in over fifty years, first woman and first person of color to fly to the Moon, Apollo 13's distance record shattered. Those milestones matter. But they are not why we can't stop watching.

The real story is not what this crew achieved. It is how they carried themselves while achieving it. And that distinction is everything.

When Everyone Can Do the Job, What Gets You the Job Changes

Here is a fun fact that reframes the entire Artemis narrative. NASA does not have a shortage of people who can fly this mission. One astronaut class drew over 18,000 applicants; the most recent, in 2025, drew more than 8,000. Ten were selected. The technical bar is high, obviously. But it is also, at this level, a given. Everyone who makes it to the final rounds is brilliant.

So if many people can do the job, why these four?

Because NASA has been asking a question for decades that most organizations still do not take seriously: what do you select for when everyone in the room is already extraordinary?

The answer, backed by decades of research, is that you start selecting for something else. NASA developed the Astronaut Personal Characteristics Inventory to measure not just achievement drive but interpersonal orientation. The finding was consistent: astronauts who scored high on both were the ones their peers rated as top performers. Not the smartest. Not the most decorated. The ones who were smart and easy to be in a room with. The European Space Agency found the same thing from the other direction: candidates who washed out scored higher on neuroticism and lower on agreeableness.

NASA even assesses for "followership," which is a word that would get you laughed out of most corporate talent reviews, but which turns out to be mission-critical when four people are sharing a space the size of a large SUV for ten days. Every astronaut must demonstrate the ability to lead in one context and defer in another, sometimes within the same hour. For longer missions, the ideal profile gets even more specific: emotionally steady, easy to work with, and, delightfully, not the loudest person in the room. The person who connects without dominating. Who talks when it matters and listens when it matters more.

Most organizations hire for visible achievement and then cross their fingers on interpersonal dynamics. NASA flips that entirely. It assumes the technical bar will be met, and then selects deliberately for how people will function together under pressure. When excellence becomes abundant, character becomes the tiebreaker.

And then they put those people on live television for ten days. What could go wrong?

Nothing, as it turns out. Everything went right.

The Earth's Best Dopamine Hit

The crew named their spacecraft Integrity. Not "Eagle." Not "Freedom." Not something that sounds good on a bumper sticker. Integrity: trust, honesty, accountability, teamwork. They said so explicitly. And then, remarkably, they lived it. On camera. For ten days. While the toilet broke.

When Merriam-Webster, of all institutions, asked Koch to describe the experience of being farther from Earth than any human in history, she did not reach for a superlative. She reached for a value. "Humility," she said, and then named not her own achievement but the history, the people forgotten who got them here, including the civil rights movement and everyone who built the hardware, put on harnesses, and tested every valve. This is the first woman to fly to the Moon, and when the dictionary asked her for a word, she chose one that celebrated everyone else.

When Glover was asked about being the first Black man to fly to the Moon, he could have claimed that milestone. Instead, he gave it away. This is not "Black history" or "women’s history," he said. It is human history. Before the crew lost radio contact behind the far side, he told Earth: "To all of you down there on Earth and around Earth, we love you from the Moon." Ground control replied: "Houston copies. We’ll see you on the other side." If you did not get chills reading that, let’s talk about this.

Social media did something it almost never does: it paused. TikTok threads filled with people watching a NASA engineer, an immigrant woman who worked on the rocket's engines, forget to pop her champagne because she was too overwhelmed by what she helped build. One commenter wrote: "I wish this were the point of social media." Yep, this is exactly why I'm here. A kid at Kennedy Space Center, asked by a reporter why he loved space, captured the whole mood in six words: "We're going back to the frickin' Moon." NASA's administrator promised him a bag of gear. The internet decided to be its best self. Turns out all it needed was four people modeling what that looks like.

What They Actually Did (That No One Is Analyzing)

Here is where I want to go deeper than the viral moments, because the viral moments are symptoms. The cause is more interesting.

Look at how this crew chose their language, in every instance, under every kind of pressure, with every kind of audience.

When the President of the United States called to congratulate them, Hansen, the Canadian on an American spacecraft during a period of acute tension between the two countries, used his moment at the microphone to thank the United States for the kind of leadership that "brings other countries along with it." He could have been careful. He was generous instead. That is a diplomatic choice, made in real time, with the whole world listening. Most trained diplomats do not pull that off. An astronaut in a floating tin can did.

When Koch described the meaning of the mission, she did not talk about her place in history. She called the Artemis program "a relay race" and revealed that the crew had bought actual batons to hand to the next crew. "Every single thing that we do is with them in mind," she said. She then explained that instead of accepting workarounds when systems malfunctioned, the crew pushed to fix everything, not for themselves, but so the next team would inherit something better. That is not ambition. That is stewardship. And it is wildly rare.

When Wiseman, the commander, described the most meaningful part of the mission, he did not talk about the distance record or the eclipse or the far side of the Moon. He talked about hearing his crewmates on the phone with their families. "Hearing your crew mates giggling and crying, and just gasping and listening and loving their families from afar," he said. He named the thing that most leaders would edit out: tenderness as a feature of high performance, not a distraction from it.

And Glover, before the crew disappeared behind the Moon and lost all contact with Earth, chose to spend his last audible words not on a technical update or a patriotic flourish but on a reminder about love. Koch told reporters the crew's bond felt like family. "We are bumping into each other 100% of the time," she said. "Everything we do in here is a four-person activity." During the communication blackout behind the Moon, all four shared maple cookies Hansen had brought, took a few minutes to reflect on where they were, and then went back to work.

None of this was scripted. None of it was prompted by a communications team. Every one of these moments was a choice made by people who had been selected, trained, and formed to operate with emotional precision under pressure, and who chose, again and again, to lead with vulnerability, generosity, and attention to others.

This Is the Difference. And the Whole World Felt It.

The Artemis II crew was not performing leadership. They were practicing presence. And there is a difference, even if most organizations have never been forced to articulate it.

Performance is strategic. It communicates at an audience. Presence is relational. It communicates with people. Performance optimizes for message. Presence optimizes for trust. In a media environment saturated with talking points, brand management, and carefully curated "authenticity" (a word that has been strip-mined of all meaning), this crew did something disarmingly simple: they said what they actually felt, in real time, and let the moment be bigger than they were.

That is why people on social media cannot look away. Not because these astronauts are doing something spectacular, though they are. Because they are doing something rare: leading without performing. And we are so starved for it that when it shows up at a quarter-million miles from Earth, millions of people feel it in their chest.

Soft Power at 250,000 Miles

Joseph Nye, who passed away almost exactly a year ago after a lifetime of shaping how we understand influence, defined soft power as the ability to attract and persuade rather than coerce. But attraction is not abstract. It is built through signals.

What Artemis is signaling is this: here is a group of people entrusted with something enormous, and here is how they treat each other while doing it. Not a speech. Not a policy. A team. And crucially, a team that feels believable.

That signal travels. Psychologists call what the astronauts and millions of viewers are experiencing the "overview effect," the profound shift that comes from seeing Earth whole and borderless from space. But what is happening on the ground is its own kind of overview effect: a brief, collective realization that we are capable of more than our feeds suggest. The joy so many of us are feeling is not passive. It is a recognition. These four people are modeling something we are hungry for, and the fact that we can feel it from a quarter-million miles away tells us something important about what we value when performance is stripped down to character.

A machine can summarize a meeting. It cannot choose to spend its last words before a communication blackout talking about love. It cannot name a crater after someone's dead wife and mean it. It cannot buy batons for a crew it will never fly with. It cannot choose humility over heroism when the dictionary literally asks you for a word.

The Artemis II crew just demonstrated, from farther away than any humans have ever been, the most important leadership insight of the decade: when excellence becomes abundant, character is what compounds. The interaction between people is not a byproduct of the mission. It is the system. And the most powerful thing you can do in any room, or any capsule, is be the kind of person other people trust when there is no signal and no script.

Tomorrow, they splash down off San Diego. They will come home to a world that, for ten days, remembered what it feels like to root for the same team. That feeling, washing over all of us right now? That is soft power. No one had to sell it to us, and wow did we want it, embrace it, and bask in it.

item.title: Artemis II is a better use of money than welfare or bombs | Your Turn - USA Today
item.description:
Artemis II is a better use of money than welfare or bombs | Your Turn

'As someone who witnessed the original moon landing in 1969, I'm ecstatic to see America reengaging in human space exploration. It is our very nature to grow, to expand, to learn.'

Artemis II marked the first crewed moon mission in more than 50 years, in which we traveled farther from Earth than ever before and got our first look with the naked eye at parts of our natural satellite's far side.

The trip was a prelude to what NASA says will be a moon landing by 2028 and then a constantly inhabited lunar base.

All of this will cost billions of dollars. And it will give us access to hundreds of billions of dollars in untapped resources, such as rare elements, scientists say.

The question is: Is it all worth it? Both to the taxpayers and to the astronauts taking the risk?

For opinions on that, we turned to you, our USA TODAY readers. Your answers ranged from serious skepticism of the costly program to excitement over our continued exploration.

Here's a sampling of what you said below in our latest installment of Forum. Look for more opportunities to weigh in at usatoday.com/forum, leave us a voicemail at (202) 655-3923 or drop us a note at forum@usatoday.com.

Space exploration is a better use of public dollars than many things

The Artemis II mission is amazing and awe-inspiring. I've been following the Artemis program since it started and eagerly await the next missions. These missions represent the best things humanity has ever done.

Space exploration is a better use of public money than anything else our government spends. We waste trillions of dollars on welfare and fraud and bombs, when we could be exploring the cosmos and moving humanity forward. NASA's budget should be several times larger.

Both NASA and private companies have a role here. NASA is great at funding large missions that no one else can afford, such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the International Space Station. SpaceX and Blue Origin are innovating and driving down the costs of going to space. Space is big, and there is room for everyone who wants to participate.

We should absolutely be colonizing the moon first, then Mars. There has always been a human drive to explore and reach for the stars. We can't stop reaching just because the next step is a little harder than the one before.

— Dawn Smith, Texas

Those billions of dollars would be better spent cleaning up Earth

My thought is that the billions of dollars this mission costs are a total waste of resources. We know there is nothing out there for humans, so stop wasting our time and resources. Space is just a wasteful boondoggle!

Instead of wasting money where humans cannot survive, redirect those funds to reforestation and ocean cleanup. We need to care for our planet because it's our only chance.

The truth is, private space companies wouldn't exist without taxpayer dollars and neither would NASA. All of this space nonsense should be stopped immediately, and those resources should go to our planet and its problems here.

America has nearly $40 trillion in debt and cannot afford pointless boondoggles.

There is no intelligent life anywhere humans can reach. We know there is no life in our solar system. Everything else is science fiction. There has never been one shred of evidence supporting intelligent life anywhere but Earth. I'll believe it when I see it, but so far zero evidence.

— Jeffrey Moore, Nevada

Americans need health care and housing ‒ not space photos

At this time in this world, I don’t think it is worth the cost. How does the moon mission help get food prices lower, insurance fixed or get other costs lowered? It does not. How does the moon mission help end this Iran war of choice? It does not. How does this moon mission better the lives of the American people? It does not.

While I applaud the brave astronauts and believe in scientific exploration, I feel this is the wrong time. Our country needs to focus on bettering the living conditions of the American people.

When so many average Americans are hurting due to high prices, I don’t think our tax dollars are being well spent. Funding should go to help the average American, to bolster Social Security and Medicare.

Let SpaceX and Blue Origin drive space travel. NASA should have a smaller role until our country is back to normal. I see no point in humans colonizing the moon or Mars. What is the point? For exploration, yes. For colonizing, no.

— Joy Harris, California

Scientific exploration is the best use of public money

As someone who witnessed the original moon landing in 1969, I'm ecstatic to see America reengaging in human space exploration. It is our very nature to grow, to expand, to learn.

Scientific pursuits are one of the best uses of public money. It grows us all, expands our horizons and teaches us more about ourselves. What may seem like a "waste" today can have unforeseen benefits for mankind.

While private exploration and programs are laudable, only governments can, and should, fund something so costly and technology-intensive, because it benefits all people and the planet.

We should absolutely colonize other planets. To grow, to learn, to have the opportunity to adapt and find out more about ourselves and the galaxy around us is what makes humans grow beyond who we are today.

I believe aliens do exist, but I can't even begin to speculate what form they will take, how they will interpret us, and what we will do if we ever come together. My best hope is that they will help us find the skills intellectually, socially and technologically to solve so many of our current problems and shortcomings.

— Scott Piepenburg, Pennsylvania

To explore is to be human

Humans are meant to explore. It is a part of our DNA. To search out and seek to know. It is time to go on. We are all on a spaceship called Earth. Space exploration helps us to remember that we are all human.

Space exploration is a good use of public money. But it will require private money and firms working together to put a base on the moon and to develop the technology needed to go on. Private companies should be involved in space travel and exploration under the leadership of NASA. This is so big it will require private and public money and effort.

The new technologies that will be developed will benefit all humans.

We should colonize the moon and Mars. Who knows what potential benefits we might discover? And it pulls us together and helps us to see just how small we are. The science that might be unlocked. And the fact that humans can work together to the benefit of one another.

Our universe is so vast that life can exist elsewhere. We have to be pretty close-minded to think otherwise. So life outside our world is possible.

— Rick Jones, Ohio

item.title: What the Artemis II astronauts shared in first remarks after return to Earth - CNN
item.description:
It was a hero’s welcome for the four-personArtemis II crew following a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean on Friday evening.

The astronautsarrived Saturday at Ellington Field at Johnson Space Center in Houston to cheers, a standing ovation and hugs from NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. The crewmates reunited with their families at the site for the first time since their historic 10-day journey around the moon concluded.

Isaacman referred to the mission as “the greatest adventure in human history.”

The crew — NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen — completed a record-breaking lunar flyby. The astronauts traveled deeper into space than any human had ventured before. The Artemis II mission was a test flight, serving as an experiment to lay the groundwork for future missions. But the moment of reuniting with their loved ones has been among the most anticipated steps of the crew’s journey.

“Victor, Christina and Jeremy, we are, we are bonded forever, and no one down here is ever going to know what the four of us just went through,” Wiseman said. “And it was the most special thing that will ever happen in my life.”

No place like planet Earth

Wiseman acknowledged that no one will truly know what the crew’s families went through.

“This was not easy being 200,000-plus miles away from home,” Wiseman said. “Like, before you launch it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth, and when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.” Wiseman was visibly choked up, and the four crewmembers stood to hug on stage.

Glover admitted he has not fully processed the entire mission and “what we just did” yet, but was full of gratitude.

“When this started, I wanted to thank God in public, and I want to thank God again, because even bigger than my challenge trying to describe what we went through, the gratitude of seeing what we saw, doing what we did, and being with who I was with, it’s too big to just be in one body,” Glover said.

“And I wanted to thank our families for everything,” he added. “I love you, but not just those five beautiful cocoa-skinned ladies right there,” Glover said, gesturing to his family. “All of you.”

‘You are a crew’

Koch shared that her nurse on the Navy recovery ship asked her for a hug last night, one of many great “human moments” that began and ended the mission, she said. Artemis II truly taught her the meaning of what it is to be part of a crew, Koch said.

“A crew is a group that is in it all the time, no matter what, that is stroking together every minute with the same purpose, that is willing to sacrifice silently for each other, that gives grace, that holds accountable,” Koch said. “A crew has the same cares and the same needs, and a crew is inescapably beautifully, dutifully linked.”

She said one of her strongest revelations came while observing Earth appear tiny through the window of Orion, and all of the blackness around it.

“I know I haven’t learned everything that this journey has yet to teach me,” Koch said. “But there’s one new thing I know, and that is planet Earth: You are a crew.”

Shared humanity and family ties

Hansen also noted that the human experience has been an extraordinary one for him and his crewmates — and seemed thrilled to learn it was the same way for everyone on Earth who followed the mission.

“We have a term in our crew that we coined a long time ago, the ‘joy train,’” Hansen said. “And it sounds like you saw a lot of joy up there. There was a lot of joy. We’re not always on the joy train, this crew, there are many times we’re not on the joy train, but we are committed to getting back on the joy train as soon as we can. And that is a useful life skill for any team trying to get something done.”

Hansen asked his crewmates to stand with him as he talked about love.

“What you saw was a group of people who loved contributing, having meaningful contribution and extracting joy out of that,” Hansen said. “And what we’ve been hearing is that was something special for you to witness. I would suggest to you that when you look up here, you’re not looking at us. We are a mirror reflecting you, and if you like what you see, then just look a little deeper. This is you.”

During the trip, the astronauts were able to speak with their spouses and children via brief, remote calls. Wiseman, the mission commander, said the experience of listening to his crewmates’ conversations while crammed together aboard the 16.5-foot-wide (5-meter-wide) Orion spacecraft was a remarkable bonding experience.

“Hearing your crewmates giggling and crying and just gasping and listening and loving their families from afar,” Wiseman said, has been the “neatest” bonding experience.

“Family is so important to all four of us, and that has been amazing,” Wiseman said during an April 8 dispatch from Orion.

Wiseman said he was moved to tears and could hardly speak when he first connected with his daughters from space. He is a widower, and during the mission, the crew proposed naming a lunar crater for his late wife, Carroll.

Looking to the future

Wiseman’s final words Saturday were for the NASA astronauts that had gathered in the auditorium.

“It is time to go and be ready,” Wiseman said, speaking of future space exploration. “Because it takes courage. It takes determination. And you all are freaking going, and we are going to be standing there supporting you every single step of the way in every possible way possible.”

Isaacman said that the Artemis II mission will always be remembered because it’s the moment when the crew, and people around the world, saw the moon again and “where childhood dreams became missions.” And it paves the way for future missions like Artemis III, expected to launch in 2027. The administrator noted that assembly of the Artemis III vehicle, and the announcement of that mission’s crew, will occur soon.

“The next crew will begin preparing to play their part as we return to the lunar surface, we build the base and we never give up the moon again,” Isaacman said.

Vanessa Wyche, director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said the “moon joy” spread by the crew will empower and inspire a new generation to believe that their dreams are possible.

“It will lead countless students to become the next scientists, engineers, inventors, mathematicians and astronauts who will dare to forge new frontiers in space, and push the boundaries of what’s possible for the benefit of all,” Wyche said. “We often say that we stand on the shoulders of giants, and after seeing them return from this mission, I have to say their shoulders now seem even broader for the next generation to stand on.”
